items.t: PepsiCo Stock And Other Dividend Names Worth Watching As Rate Hike Risks Return
sum: The Fed is hinting at more rate hikes, markets are bracing for higher borrowing costs, and suddenly the calm, dividend-paying corner of the market looks a lot more interesting. Income-focused large caps with moderate yields and sturdier balance sheets can feel like a hiding place when policy stays tight and volatility picks up. This article walks through three stocks from our value and dividend screener that appear closely tied to this new rate reality.

The three examples below are just a sample, as the full screen pulled up 9 more large caps with income, value and balance sheet profiles that tell similarly compelling stories. If you want to move beyond a short list and actively sort through the full universe, head straight to the US Large-Cap Value and Dividend Stocks screener to identify, compare and analyze candidates that best fit your own conviction and risk tolerance.
Overview: PepsiCo is a global food and beverage company that sells branded snacks and drinks to retailers, foodservice outlets and consumers worldwide.

Operations: PepsiCo generates most of its revenue from PepsiCo Beverages North America at US$29.5b and PepsiCo Foods North America at US$27.5b, with meaningful contributions from EMEA at US$19.3b and Latin America Foods at US$11.6b.

For an income screen built around durability in a higher-rate world, PepsiCo fits neatly, and AshleighG, a Simply Wall St Community investor who wrote the Narrative, argues that the real question now is how its next wave of products reshapes a very mature portfolio.

"The company is pushing into functional and health-focused drinks with the acquisition of Poppi (prebiotic soda), ownership of Bubly (sparkling water), and a partnership with Celsius (including Rockstar energy drinks)."
What really matters for dividend-focused investors is how one quiet shift in PepsiCo’s business mix ultimately feeds through to future cash generation.

PepsiCo stock gains as North American job cuts target simpler operations
sum: PepsiCo is turning to a North American restructuring as weak beverage demand, softer premium-snack sales and elevated input costs weigh on its home market. Reuters reported on November 9 that the company plans job cuts in its North American food and beverage business, with changes expected during the following week.

The report said PepsiCo North America Chief Executive Ram Krishnan told employees that the goal was to simplify the unit, move faster and execute better while continuing to invest in growth. The Wall Street Journal had reported that the reduction could affect around 1,000 roles. PepsiCo has not publicly detailed the distribution of the affected positions in the Reuters report.

The workforce action comes after PepsiCo lowered its full-year earnings forecast in October. Reuters linked the pressure to sluggish soda sales, weaker demand for higher-priced snacks and rising input costs, particularly in North America.

PepsiCo's North American beverage volume fell 2 percent in the third quarter, while food volume was flat, according to the company's recent operating update as reported by CNBC. The restructuring therefore addresses both organizational complexity and a demand environment that has made volume recovery more difficult.

PepsiCo stock traded at 129.84 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 17:05 CET on Thursday, November 12, 2026, 1.98 percent above the Xetra close of 127.32 euros from Wednesday, November 11. Compared with the 127.29-euro quote in the previous report on November 11 at 17:01 CET, the stock was 2.00 percent higher, a separate comparison from the Xetra session move.

The latest restructuring gives management a concrete operating response, but it does not establish a recovery in volumes or margins. For investors, the key measure will be whether simpler reporting lines and faster decisions translate into stronger sales execution while preserving investment in brands and innovation.
Broader conditions for US-listed consumer companies can be followed through the S&P 500 market environment.

Can PepsiCo (NASDAQ:PEP) Steady Its Drinks Business With KFC Deal?
PepsiCo's Eight-Market KFC Renewal Overshadowed by Indian Label Fight and North American Restructuri
sum: PepsiCo is pressing ahead on three fronts at once — expanding a restaurant pour agreement, defending its labeling practices in an Indian courtroom, and preparing a sweeping reorganization of its North American operations.

The beverage and snacks giant confirmed on Friday that it has extended its drinks partnership with KFC across eight countries: Germany, France, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium, the United Kingdom, Australia and India. The renewed tie-up spans both European markets and the Asia-Pacific region, keeping PepsiCo products flowing through KFC outlets in each of the named countries.

Far from the KFC deal, PepsiCo finds itself embroiled in a legal dispute in India over how caffeinated beverages are marketed. On November 4, the country's food safety regulator accused PepsiCo and Monster Beverage of misleading consumers by branding such products as "Energy Drinks."

The allegation was lodged in court filings through which the authority is defending India's restrictions on that labeling. PepsiCo is among the companies challenging the curbs — setting up a clash between the regulator and some of the biggest names in the global beverage industry.

Closer to home, PepsiCo is planning to cut roughly 1,000 jobs in its North American food and beverage business, according to Bloomberg Law, which reported the figure. The company has not publicly confirmed the number, so it reflects the scale of the planned measure as reported by Bloomberg Law rather than an official company statement.

Ram Krishnan, who heads the North America division, told employees that the changes are designed to create simpler structures and clearer lines of responsibility in parts of the organization. According to Reuters, the organizational changes are also intended to speed up decision-making, and they are expected to be rolled out as soon as next week.

The stock's recent run hit a pause on the day the KFC extension was announced. PepsiCo shares fell 0.6% to €127.88, retreating from the prior session's close of €129.82, when the stock had added 0.9% and extended a positive stretch stretching back seven trading days.

sum: PepsiCo Inc. stock (PEP) is on track for its worst month since May, with shares down more than 7% in September, as the company adjusts pricing and prepares for fiscal third-quarter (Q3) 2026 results. Meanwhile, Colombia announced PepsiCo will invest $1 billion over five years to expand production, modernize operations and strengthen distribution.
PepsiCo stock edged 0.5% lower overnight, ahead of Monday. The stock has been declining for five straight weeks.
On Sept.27, Colombia President Abelardo De La Espriella announced on X that PepsiCo will invest $1 billion.

“It's a resounding decision: to expand production, modernize its operations, and strengthen distribution in the country. Confidence is shown through investment. This commitment boosts employment, supports more than 2,000 farmers, and strengthens Colombian shopkeepers.”

For PepsiCo, the investment shows its long-term focus on Latin America. Expanding production and upgrading operations could help the company meet local demand, while a stronger distribution network could increase its reach among small neighborhood stores.

The pledge is one of the most important corporate commitments the new Colombian government has secured. It arrives as PepsiCo adjusts its pricing at home and prepares to report Q3 earnings on Oct. 8, giving investors a view of where the company is placing its long-term bets.

Last week, a Bloomberg report said PepsiCo plans to raise prices on some chips, sodas, and dips after cutting prices earlier this year. Chip prices could rise by low-to-mid single-digit percentages, though PepsiCo says they will remain below pre-cut levels. The company is trying to balance affordability with rising costs.

PepsiCo Slims Down in North America to Survive: 1,000 Jobs Cut, Full-Year Guidance Already Lowered
sum: PepsiCo (PEP) has decided to cut about 1,000 positions in North America to streamline its organization and bring its beverage and food teams closer together, in a bid to reignite growth in its core market where momentum has stalled. Ram Krishnan, CEO of PepsiCo North America, sent a letter to employees on the 9th explaining the move, with the layoffs expected to be carried out over the coming week.

According to Krishnan's letter, the company's vision for its North American business is to "build a stronger, more future-fit business that delivers industry-leading growth," and to get there, "we need to be faster, more closely connected, more capable, and continue to invest in growth — in our people, our capabilities and our brands." The letter was obtained by foreign media and subsequently reported by multiple financial news outlets, with the layoff scale at about 1,000 people.

According to regulatory filings, as of December 27, 2025, PepsiCo employed about 306,000 people globally, including about 125,000 in the United States. While this round of adjustments represents a limited share of the overall workforce, it is concentrated in North America, the company's most critical profit engine, making the signal more significant than the numbers themselves.
Core Market Volumes Stall, Price Cuts and Promotions Fail to Help

The layoffs did not come out of nowhere. In October, PepsiCo lowered its full-year 2026 profit outlook, citing weak North American market conditions. In the third quarter, North America beverage volumes fell 2% year over year, while North America food volumes were merely flat. With both pillars losing momentum simultaneously, the strategy of relying on price cuts and increased marketing to revive demand appeared inadequate.

CFO Steve Schmidt acknowledged on the earnings call that the company had indeed tried price cuts and expanded marketing spending to boost sales, but "the turnaround is taking longer than expected." The remark amounted to an admission that short-term promotional measures cannot solve the structural problems on the demand side.
The headwinds facing PepsiCo extend beyond the shelf.

PepsiCo Cuts 2026 Profit Growth Guidance as Gatorade Powder Push Tests Demand
sum: PepsiCo trimmed its full-year 2026 outlook for adjusted, currency-neutral earnings per share growth to 1%–2%, down from its prior target, disclosing the revision alongside third-quarter 2026 results on October 8. Reuters attributed the cut to sluggish North American demand and a recovery running behind schedule.
The guidance covers expected profit growth for the full year, while the pressures Reuters described center on demand and the pace of improvement in North America specifically.

Barclays followed with a lower price objective on October 12, reducing its target to $126 from $133 while keeping an "Equal Weight" rating on the shares. The softer number therefore came without any change to the firm's investment stance.
Friday's session saw the stock slip 0.4%. Over 30 days, however, the shares have climbed 15% — a move that cannot be read as a documented response to the October guidance reduction.

On Tuesday the company pointed to rising US sales and wider distribution for its Gatorade and Propel powders in 2026, shifting the debate toward whether additional points of sale can sustain higher demand. Management also flagged an expanded powder lineup spanning Gatorade, Propel and Gatorlyte. For investors, the question is the quality of that expansion: extra offerings create opportunity only if consumers keep coming back for them.

Sell-through is the real test. PepsiCo cites both higher sales and broader availability, and the valuation case hinges on whether demand holds up once distribution has been widened. A larger retail footprint makes the products easier to find; the economics improve if that translates into repeat purchases and if the added items contribute to the bottom line. Such an outcome would support the growth strategy — provided PepsiCo backs it with further business results.

Product and distribution expansion reinforce each other. According to media reports, a PepsiCo research and development executive also outlined the company's strategy for functional foods and its growing protein and fiber portfolio, widening the avenues for growth if the offerings resonate with consumers.

PepsiCo stock faces fresh scrutiny over dividend coverage
sum: PepsiCo stock is facing a renewed investor debate over dividend coverage after the company lowered its 2026 earnings-growth outlook. A Ground News summary of a 24/7 Wall St. analysis published on October 23 said higher input costs had made the dividend burden a more important question for investors.

The analysis focused on PepsiCo's plan to return 7.9 billion US dollars through dividends this year. It argued that free cash flow coverage was thin, making the company's ability to protect shareholder distributions more dependent on operating improvement and cost control.

PepsiCo's latest quarterly update delivered a mixed operating picture. Revenue increased 5.6 percent to 25.27 billion US dollars, while core earnings per share rose 2 percent to 2.34 US dollars. The company nevertheless reduced its 2026 core earnings-growth outlook to 2.5 percent to 3.5 percent and said North American margin pressure would continue.

The contrast matters for income-focused investors. Sales growth can support the payout over time, but weaker underlying profit expansion leaves less room to absorb higher ingredients, packaging, distribution and marketing costs. The company also faces subdued demand in North America, where management is trying to improve execution across its food and beverage businesses.

PepsiCo has said it will pursue additional structural cost reductions and use some of the savings to support advertising, innovation and operational improvements. That approach could help preserve the brands and distribution capabilities that underpin the dividend, but it also creates an execution test: savings must offset cost inflation without weakening demand-generation spending.

The dividend question therefore turns less on one quarter's reported earnings than on the conversion of revenue into recurring cash flow. Investors will be watching North American volumes, pricing, operating margins and the pace of productivity gains in upcoming reports.

Despite this, Wall Street analysts have recently lowered price targets, reflecting caution regarding the sustainability of volume momentum and rising input costs. While consensus remains a Moderate Buy with a target of $163.77, the company faces skepticism over its pace of recovery. Investors are looking to the Q2 earnings report on July 9 for confirmation that volume growth persists, serving as a critical catalyst for near-term price appreciation.

TradingKey - PepsiCo (NASDAQ: PEP) shares are trading around $143, up roughly 2% on the day, but the stock still has plenty of ground to recover. Even after today's bounce, it's sitting about 11% below its all-time high above $159 reached earlier this year and only 6% above its 52-week low of $132.96.

The drop finally makes one of the market's most recognized Dividend Kings more appealing to long-term investors. The real issue now is whether this recovery will be the initial phase of a longer recovery or just a pause prior to another downward turn.

The first-quarter '26 results (on April 16) continue to be the cornerstone of the investment thesis. Revenue increased 8.5% YoY to $19.44 billion and core EPS of $1.61 exceeded expectations by almost 4%. On a GAAP basis, earnings rose 27% to $1.70 per share.
But the biggest lesson was not revenue or earnings – it was growth in volume.

PepsiCo Foods North America reported a 2% volume increase and a 4% unit growth, bringing them closer to adding around 300 million additional consumption occasions, compared to the previous year. One of the best indicators that the company is doing the right things in terms of focusing on smaller packages and value add products is the fact that it is drawing back price-conscious consumers that were previously trading down. The next quarterly reporting period will be the proving ground to see if that momentum can be maintained or it's just a one-quarter bounce.
Management also provided another boost to income investors' confidence.

PepsiCo Secures 11-Year Taco Bell Deal Through 2036, Rebounding After KFC's Coca-Cola Shift
sum: PepsiCo Inc. (PEP) shares climbed Thursday after the beverage giant said it had locked in an 11-year extension of its fountain rights at Taco Bell, keeping its drinks in more than 8,200 U.S. restaurants through 2036 and easing fears that other chains under the same parent could follow KFC to Coca-Cola Co. (KO).

The stock rose about 2.5% to 3% in intraday trading, according to market data cited in reports on the announcement. The agreement covers participating Taco Bell, Taco Bell Cantina and Live Más Cafe locations nationwide, and preserves PepsiCo's international distribution at the chain in Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Thailand.

The timing matters. The renewal landed one week after KFC said it would drop Pepsi as its U.S. beverage supplier and switch to Coca-Cola across roughly 3,700 domestic locations beginning in January. Both KFC and Taco Bell are owned by Yum! Brands Inc. (YUM), the company PepsiCo spun off in 1997 after years of owning the restaurant group outright.

Taco Bell is the more valuable of the two domestic concepts by volume. The chain generated $17 billion in U.S. system-wide sales last year, against roughly $5 billion at KFC, making the renewal a larger prize than the contract PepsiCo lost.

PepsiCo framed the deal as a validation of a relationship that has produced exclusive menu items rather than a defensive maneuver. The company said the agreement creates room for further beverage innovation and consumer loyalty around brands including Mountain Dew and Gatorade, and both parties pledged to keep developing co-branded products.

That pipeline has a track record. Mountain Dew Baja Blast, created for Taco Bell, has grown into a $1 billion brand for PepsiCo, and Doritos Locos Tacos became one of the chain's best-known launches. The new term runs to 2036 and includes plans for additional Doritos Locos Tacos flavors.

Beverages have become a strategic growth lever for Taco Bell, which is targeting $5 billion in beverage revenue by 2030. The chain introduced its premium Refrescas line last year to capture between-meal demand, and further expansion is expected through new Baja Blast variants, including a limited-time pink lemonade developed with singer Olivia Rodrigo.

sum: PepsiCo slashed its earnings outlook Thursday, but CNBC's Jim Cramer sees reasons to be more optimistic about the struggling beverage and snack giant.

The company reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and revenue, but cut its full-year profit forecast as higher costs and investments to revive demand weighed on margins. Shares rallied 3% following the report, as investors focused on improving sales trends and a guidance cut that had been widely anticipated.

"It's far too big of a leap to say that PepsiCo is fully out of the woods here, not when there are so many secular challenges that they're facing," the "Mad Money" host said. However, given the reason for the forecast cut and the stock's relatively low valuation, "I'm feeling a lot better about this story. You could do a lot worse than buying some PepsiCo down here."

PepsiCo shares have struggled since hitting an all-time high in May 2023, before concerns about the impact of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs would have on snack consumption began to ripple across Wall Street. More recently, rising inflation, oil prices and interest rates added to the pressure, sending PepsiCo shares down nearly 10% in September alone. The stock closed Wednesday at its lowest level since April 2020.
Cramer said the positive stock reaction came down to two factors: improving sales momentum and an earnings-guidance cut that was already largely priced into the stock.
"Wall Street didn't care about the lowered earnings forecast because everyone knew this was inevitable," he said.
PepsiCo's new earnings forecast is for growth in the range of 2.5% to 3.5%, down from 5% to 7%.

sum: PepsiCo reported second-quarter results on Thursday that beat revenue forecasts but fell slightly short on adjusted earnings, as weakness in North American food and beverage sales offset strong performance abroad.

On an adjusted basis, the company earned $2.20 per share, one cent below the $2.21 consensus estimate tracked by CNBC. Total net revenue of $24.18 billion represented a 6.4% year-over-year increase and cleared the $23.95 billion Wall Street target. Stripping out currency movements, acquisitions and divestitures, organic revenue climbed 2.4%.

Geographically, the picture was split. Overseas divisions — including Asia Pacific Foods, International Beverages Franchise, and Europe, Middle East and Africa — all recorded organic volume gains, making international operations the company's main source of momentum. At home, the beverages unit suffered a 4% volume drop and the convenient foods segment ended the quarter flat.

"Our North America business was softer than we anticipated in the second quarter, and we now expect a more gradual improvement in performance trends for the balance of this year," Chief Financial Officer Steve Schmitt said in prepared remarks.

Chairman and CEO Ramon Laguarta pointed to tighter consumer budgets as a headwind. "Results were tempered in the quarter as U.S. food and beverage category performance moderated with consumer budgets tightening due to rising inflationary pressures," he said in prepared remarks.

Core operating profit rose 4% to $4.07 billion, while core operating margin narrowed by 40 basis points to 16.8%, reflecting cost pressures that partially offset productivity gains and pricing actions.

The company has been working to reverse persistent volume declines in North America. Price reductions of up to 15% on Lay's, Tostitos, Doritos and Cheetos were rolled out in February in an effort to win back shoppers, and the company has undertaken branding overhauls on flagship products such as Gatorade and Lay's. Activist investor Elliott Investment Management has pushed the company to reduce prices on selected products and expand more affordable pack sizes, according to Barron's.

The sudden downward pressure and intraday volatility on PepsiCo's shares are primarily driven by a broader macroeconomic shift following the Federal Reserve's latest monetary policy meeting. While the central bank decided to hold interest rates steady under its newly appointed leadership, the accompanying Summary of Economic Projections took a surprisingly hawkish turn. This hawkish stance has triggered a widespread repricing across the equity market, disproportionately impacting high-yielding, defensive consumer staples like PepsiCo. When interest rates remain elevated or are projected to rise, the relative appeal of traditional dividend-paying stocks diminishes as investors find safer, competitive yields in fixed-income assets.

Adding to the macro headwinds, Wall Street analysts have recently taken a more cautious stance on the snack and beverage giant. Various investment firms, including Piper Sandler and TD Cowen, trimmed their target prices for the stock. These downgrades highlight growing concerns over persistent input cost pressures, particularly related to packaging and raw materials like aluminum and oil derivatives, which are projected to impact the company's cost structures well into next year. Furthermore, slower-than-expected distribution momentum in PepsiCo's core salty snacks division continues to weigh on investor sentiment, creating doubts about near-term volume growth.

Undercurrents of demand elasticity and pricing power are also feeding market anxiety. Recent reports indicated that the company is preparing another round of price increases for its snack portfolio to counteract sticky inflation. items.t: 4 Stocks That Can Fund Decades of Passive Income -- Buy Them While They're Down
sum: There's only so much money to go around on Wall Street, so when some stocks go up, something else is usually going down. Investors have been all about technology and artificial intelligence stocks for the past several years, leaving some iconic consumer brand companies in the dust.

These four consumer stocks have rich histories of paying dividends and survived the test of time. They have all fallen 26% to 74% from their all-time highs. Sure, some of these companies have issues, but renowned brands don't typically drop without some adversity.
Here's why investors can buy each one while they're still down, and reasonably expect the dividends to continue pouring in for years to come.

Sporting apparel giant Nike (NKE -2.45%) has struggled for several years. Its misguided direct-to-consumer strategy opened the door for competitors and prompted Nike to fire its CEO in late 2024. Current CEO and longtime company veteran Elliott Hill is working to get Nike's wholesale relationships and product innovation back on track. China has remained a difficult market for Nike, and the stock has continued to grind lower from its 2021 high.

That said, Nike is still the top dog in the world of sports apparel. Although the company has paid and raised its dividend for 24 consecutive years, Nike's earnings have deteriorated to a troubling extent amid its struggles. The stock is more risky now, but investors have a rare opportunity to buy Nike at a 3.6% dividend yield. A yield trap? Perhaps not. Analysts see Nike's earnings rebounding to $2.40 per share by the end of its next fiscal year, which would bring that dividend back to a safe place.

Food and beverages never go out of style. That simple truth has made PepsiCo (PEP -0.96%) a Dividend King with 54 consecutive annual increases. The company owns a vast portfolio of soda and snack food brands, including Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Gatorade, Lay's, Doritos, Cheetos, Quaker, and more. These are brands people recognize and tend to reach for in the grocery store. But despite the power of these brand names, PepsiCo has struggled to grow sales over the past couple of years.
The biggest culprit could be management, which raised prices too aggressively following the COVID-19 pandemic.

Beyond product innovation, PepsiCo is pairing its growth initiatives with aggressive productivity improvements to fund investments and strengthen execution. PepsiCo also sees major opportunities tied to global events like the World Cup, where innovation, personalized marketing and occasion-based campaigns are expected to accelerate brand engagement worldwide. Wall Street is closely watching the results for signs of renewed growth momentum, particularly after activist investor Elliott Management disclosed a stake in the company and began pushing for strategic changes.

Shares of PepsiCo are up more than 8% so far in 2026, marking a rebound after a three-year losing streak. In December, the company announced adjustments to its business strategy following engagement with Elliott, a move that helped revive investor interest. PepsiCo has said it plans to rethink innovation, productivity, and affordability initiatives, with a particular focus on its North American snacks and beverages division.

Barclays raised its price target on PepsiCo to $148 from $144 and maintained an ‘Equal Weight,’ according to The Fly. The firm said that it attributes the recent "enthusiasm" in the stock to "a flight to safety" and remains concerned about company and sector-level fundamentals.

BNP Paribas upgraded PepsiCo to ‘Outperform’ from ‘Neutral’ and raised the firm’s fiscal 2027 earnings per share estimate by about 5%, noting that activist involvement at Pepsi is driving a proverbial "win-win" setup.
Wall Street expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise 4% to $28.95 billion and earnings per share to come in at $2.24, compared to $1.96 a year earlier, according to data compiled by Fiscal AI.

PepsiCo said it would offer sharper everyday value through a targeted approach to affordable price tiers by brand and channel, and the company plans to lower prices on some food items in the coming year. PepsiCo has faced intense competition from Coca-Cola in the soda segment, where Coca-Cola has gained market share.

The company said that, as part of its business review, it has decided to aggressively reduce operating costs and improve operations. It closed three manufacturing plants and shut several manufacturing lines this year.

items.t: Buy PepsiCo heading into 2026 as innovation drives earnings, says JPMorgan
sum: JPMorgan is adopting a more bullish stance on shares of PepsiCo . The bank upgraded the food and beverage giant to an overweight rating from neutral. It also lifted its December 2026 price target to $164 from $151, which implies upside of 13%. Analyst Andrea Teixeira said that she sees PepsiCo delivering earnings in the mid- to high-single digit range next year, citing more aggressive productivity targets and an improving top line. This record productivity should allow for reinvestment and a flow-through in profit, she added. PEP YTD mountain PEP YTD chart "We are upgrading PepsiCo to Overweight from Neutral as we believe an accelerated agenda of innovation and marketing spending fueled by strong productivity savings should position PEP to drive HSD total shareholder return (TSR) in 2026, which benchmarks well against high-quality peers yet at a steep high-teens discount," the analyst wrote. Teixeira also sees PepsiCo benefiting from additional shelf space and affordability initiatives next year. She called PepsiCo's 2026 guidance "constructive" alongside improving consumption trends in U.S. snacking. "Management also noted that in testing with its largest three customers over the past three months that its everyday value efforts have seen 'very good metrics' and confidence that 'volume will come,' which we take to mean that the company has seen favorable elasticities to its efforts," she added. Shares of PepsiCo have slipped 5% this year. The stock also ticked higher by around 1% after the upgrade. Most analysts covering PepsiCo are on the sidelines despite JPMorgan's rating change. Of the 26 who cover the stock, 17 rate it as a hold, LSEG data shows. Another eight assigned it a buy or strong buy rating, and one has a hold rating on the stock.
